results.title: Regular functions
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a commutative semiring $k$ and index types $\sigma$ and $\tau$, a regular function from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\tau$ is a family $F = (F_t)_{t \in \tau}$ of polynomials in the variables $X_s$, $s \in \sigma$, with coefficients in $k$.

results.title: Jacobian matrix of a regular function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Jacobian of a regular function $F = (F_j)_{j \in \tau}$ from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\tau$ is the $\tau \times \sigma$ matrix, with entries in the polynomial ring $k[X_i : i \in \sigma]$, whose entry in row $j$ and column $i$ is the formal partial derivative $\partial F_j / \partial X_i$.

results.title: Composition of regular functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For regular functions $G$ from $k^\tau$ to $k^\iota$ and $F$ from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\tau$, the composition $G \circ F$ is the regular function from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\iota$ whose $i$-th component, for $i \in \iota$, is the polynomial obtained from $G_i$ by substituting $F_t$ for the variable $X_t$ for every $t \in \tau$.

results.title: The identity is a left unit for composition
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every regular function $F$ from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\tau$, composing the identity regular function on $k^\tau$, whose components are the variables $X_t$ for $t \in \tau$, with $F$ gives $F$, that is, $\mathrm{id} \circ F = F$.

results.title: The identity is a right unit for composition
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every regular function $F$ from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\tau$, composing $F$ with the identity regular function on $k^\sigma$, whose components are the variables $X_s$ for $s \in \sigma$, gives $F$, that is, $F \circ \mathrm{id} = F$.

results.title: Associativity of composition of regular functions
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For regular functions $H$ from $k^\iota$ to $k^\kappa$, $G$ from $k^\tau$ to $k^\iota$ and $F$ from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\tau$, we have $(H \circ G) \circ F = H \circ (G \circ F)$.

results.title: Evaluation of a regular function at a point
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $k$ be a commutative semiring and let $S$ be a commutative $k$-algebra. For a regular function $F$ from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\tau$ and a point $a \in S^\sigma$, the evaluation of $F$ at $a$ is the point $F(a) \in S^\tau$ whose $t$-th coordinate, for $t \in \tau$, is the value of the polynomial $F_t$ at $a$, obtained by substituting $a_s$ for $X_s$ for every $s \in \sigma$.

results.title: Evaluation respects composition
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: Let $k$ be a commutative semiring and let $S$ be a commutative $k$-algebra. For regular functions $G$ from $k^\tau$ to $k^\iota$ and $F$ from $k^\sigma$ to $k^\tau$ and every point $a \in S^\sigma$, write $F(a) \in S^\tau$ for the evaluation of $F$ at $a$. Then evaluating the composition $G \circ F$ at $a$ gives $G(F(a))$, the evaluation of $G$ at the point $F(a)$.

results.title: Torsion-free abelian group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An abelian group $A$, written additively, is torsion-free when for every natural number $n \ne 0$ and every $a \in A$, $n a = 0$ implies $a = 0$.

results.title: Bergman's absorption question (Kourovka 17.21(a))
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for all torsion-free abelian groups $A$, $B$, $C$, if $A \cong A \oplus B \oplus C$ then $A \cong A \oplus B$.

results.title: Bergman's absorption question for isomorphic summands (Kourovka 17.21(b))
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for all torsion-free abelian groups $A$, $B$, $C$ with $B \cong C$, if $A \cong A \oplus B \oplus C$ then $A \cong A \oplus B$.

results.title: Failure of direct-summand absorption for torsion-free abelian groups
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There exist torsion-free abelian groups $A$, $B$, $C$ with $A \cong A \oplus B \oplus C$ but $A \not\cong A \oplus B$; thus the answer to Kourovka Problem 17.21(a) is negative.

results.title: Failure of direct-summand absorption with isomorphic summands
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There exist torsion-free abelian groups $A$, $B$, $C$ with $B \cong C$ and $A \cong A \oplus B \oplus C$ but $A \not\cong A \oplus B$; thus the answer to Kourovka Problem 17.21(b) is negative.

results.title: Metacyclic group

results.summary: A group $G$ is metacyclic if it has a cyclic normal subgroup $N$ such that the quotient $G/N$ is cyclic.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 15.33, with the bound $2$

results.summary: The statement that every finite $2$-group $G$ such that for all $x, y \in G$ the subgroup $\langle x, y \rangle$ generated by $x$ and $y$ is metacyclic has derived length at most $2$, that is, its second derived subgroup $G''$ is trivial.

results.title: Finite $2$-groups with metacyclic $2$-generator subgroups are metabelian (Kourovka Problem 15.33)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Finite $2$-groups with metacyclic $2$-generator subgroups are metabelian (Kourovka Problem 15.33). Let $G$ be a finite $2$-group such that for all $x, y \in G$ the subgroup $\langle x, y \rangle$ generated by $x$ and $y$ is metacyclic, that is, has a cyclic normal subgroup with cyclic quotient. Then $G$ is metabelian: its second derived subgroup $G''$ is trivial.

results.title: Choquet representation for compact sets
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a second-countable real Banach space with its Borel σ-algebra and let $K \subseteq E$ be compact. For every $x \in K$ there is a probability measure $\mu$ on $E$ such that the set $\operatorname{ext} K$ of extreme points of $K$ has $\mu(\operatorname{ext} K) = 1$, the identity map $y \mapsto y$ is Bochner integrable for $\mu$, and $\int_E y \, d\mu(y) = x$.

results.title: Choquet's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a second-countable real Banach space with its Borel σ-algebra and let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact convex set. For every $x \in K$ there is a probability measure $\mu$ on $E$ such that the set $\operatorname{ext} K$ of extreme points of $K$ has $\mu(\operatorname{ext} K) = 1$, the identity map $y \mapsto y$ is Bochner integrable for $\mu$, and $\int_E y \, d\mu(y) = x$.

results.title: Choquet's representation theorem in Banach spaces
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ be a real Banach space with its Borel σ-algebra and let $K \subseteq X$ be compact and convex. For every $x \in K$ there is a probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that the complement of the set of extreme points of $K$ has $\mu$-measure $0$ and the barycenter $\int y \, d\mu(y)$ (a Bochner integral) equals $x$.

results.title: Bauer's uniqueness theorem at extreme points
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ be a real Banach space with its Borel σ-algebra, let $K \subseteq X$ be compact and convex, and let $x$ be an extreme point of $K$. If $\mu$ is a probability measure on $X$ with $\mu(X \setminus K) = 0$ whose barycenter $\int y \, d\mu(y)$ (a Bochner integral) equals $x$, then $\mu$ is the Dirac measure at $x$.

results.title: Chung–Diaconis–Graham universal cycle conjecture
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every natural number $k$ there is a natural number $N$ such that every $n \ge N$ for which $k$ divides $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ admits a universal cycle for the $k$-subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Here $n - 1$ and $k - 1$ are truncated at $0$, so for $k = 0$ the divisibility condition reads $0 \mid 1$ and never holds.

results.title: Existence of universal cycles for $k$-subsets
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$ there is a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ for which $k$ divides $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$, there is a universal cycle for the $k$-subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Here $n - 1$ and $k - 1$ are truncated at $0$, so for $k = 0$ the divisibility condition reads $0 \mid 1$ and never holds.

results.title: Well-formed 3-dimensional matching instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A 3-dimensional matching instance $(n, T)$ is well formed when each of the three coordinates of every triple in $T$ is less than $n$.

results.title: Feasible 3-dimensional matching instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A 3-dimensional matching instance $(n, T)$ is feasible, or has a perfect matching, when there is a list $M$ of length $n$, obtained from the list of triples $T$ by deleting some of its entries, such that for each of the three coordinate positions, every natural number $a < n$ occurs in that position in exactly one triple of $M$.

results.title: 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a 3-dimensional matching instance $(n, T)$ that is well formed (every coordinate of every triple in $T$ is less than $n$) and feasible (it has a perfect matching). Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

results.title: 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING on bitstrings is in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

results.title: If P = NP then the polynomial hierarchy collapses to P
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the complexity classes P and NP are equal, then the polynomial hierarchy PH, the union of the classes $\Sigma_k^p$ over all natural numbers $k$, is equal to P.

results.title: The polynomial hierarchy is contained in PSPACE
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every decision problem in the polynomial hierarchy PH belongs to PSPACE.

Whole-graph decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices

results.title: Depth-first traversal record
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A traversal over a vertex type $V$ consists of three lists: a preorder (discovery order) list of vertices, a postorder (finish order) list of vertices, and a list of parent pairs in $V \times V$, each stored as $(\text{child}, \text{parent})$.

results.title: Left-first depth-first search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and an ordered list of roots, depth-first search processes the roots from left to right, skipping roots already visited. Visiting an unvisited vertex $v$ marks it visited and records its discovery, then processes the out-neighbours of $v$ in adjacency-list order, visiting each one not yet visited at that moment and recording $v$ as its parent, and finally…

results.title: Sequences of depth-first search machine steps
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Zero or more independent DFS machine steps.

results.title: Left-first depth-first traversals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $r = (r_1, \dots, r_k)$ be a list of root vertices. A traversal $T$ is a left-first DFS of $G$ from $r$ when some finite run of the following machine ends with an empty work list and with recorded preorder, postorder and (child, parent) list equal to those of $T$.

results.title: Executable DFS meets the left-first specification
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every ordered list of roots, the traversal computed by left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots conforms to left-first DFS for $G$ and these roots.

results.title: The left-first DFS specification determines the traversal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, fix an ordered list of roots, and let $T$ be a traversal. If $T$ conforms to left-first DFS for $G$ and these roots, then $T$ equals the traversal computed by left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots.

results.title: Depth-first search discovers only reachable vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $R$ be a list of roots. Every vertex in the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ is reachable in $G$ from some root in $R$ by a directed path (possibly of length zero).

results.title: Depth-first search discovers every reachable vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $R$ be a list of roots. If a vertex $v$ is reachable in $G$ from some root in $R$ by a directed path (possibly of length zero), then $v$ occurs in the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$.

results.title: Depth-first search discovers exactly the reachable vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. A vertex $v$ occurs in the discovery order (preorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ if and only if there is a root $r$ in $R$ from which $v$ is reachable in $G$ by a directed path of length zero or more.

results.title: Depth-first search discovers each vertex at most once
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every list $R$ of roots, the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ contains no vertex twice.

results.title: Depth-first search finishes exactly the reachable vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. A vertex $v$ occurs in the finish order (postorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ if and only if there is a root $r$ in $R$ from which $v$ is reachable in $G$ by a directed path of length zero or more.

results.title: DFS finishes each vertex at most once
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. The finish order (postorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ contains no vertex twice.

results.title: Occurring before in a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For elements $x$ and $y$ and a list $xs$, $x$ occurs before $y$ in $xs$ when there are lists $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $xs$ is the concatenation of $a$, the element $x$, $b$, the element $y$ and $c$; that is, some occurrence of $x$ lies at a strictly earlier position than some occurrence of $y$.

results.title: Parent relation of a list of pairs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $P$ of (child, parent) pairs, $p$ is a parent of $c$ in $P$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in $P$.

results.title: Roots of a DFS forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The forest roots of a traversal $T$ are the vertices of the preorder of $T$ that do not occur as the child in any (child, parent) pair recorded by $T$, listed in the order in which they occur in the preorder.

results.title: DFS forest roots are distinct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every list $r$ of root vertices, the list of forest roots of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$ contains no vertex twice.

results.title: A DFS forest root has no parent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ and $p$ be vertices. If $v$ is a forest root of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$, then $(v, p)$ is not among the (child, parent) pairs recorded by that search.

results.title: DFS parent pairs are graph edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $G$ has a directed edge from $p$ to $c$.

results.title: No vertex is recorded twice as a DFS child
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. In the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, no vertex occurs as the child of more than one entry; that is, the list of children has no repeated entries.

results.title: Every discovered vertex is a forest root or has a unique parent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex in the preorder of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$. Then $v$ is a forest root of that search, or there is exactly one vertex $p$ such that $(v, p)$ is among the (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search.

results.title: In preorder, a DFS parent precedes its child
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $p$ occurs strictly before $c$ in the discovery order (preorder) of the search.

results.title: A DFS child finishes before its parent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph with ordered adjacency lists and fix an ordered list of roots. If $(c, p)$ is one of the (child, parent) pairs recorded by the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots, then $c$ occurs before $p$ in the postorder (finish order) of that search.

results.title: Decreasing finish order
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and an ordered list of roots, the decreasing finish order is the reverse of the postorder of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from those roots: the vertices that search visits, listed from the latest finished to the earliest finished.

results.title: In decreasing finish order, a DFS parent precedes its child
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $p$ occurs strictly before $c$ in the decreasing finish order, the reverse of the finish order.

results.title: Decreasing finish order lists exactly the vertices reachable from the roots
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex. Then $v$ occurs in the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$ if and only if $v$ is reachable in $G$ from some vertex of $r$.

results.title: Decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every ordered list of roots, the decreasing finish order of the depth-first search of $G$ from those roots contains no vertex twice.

results.title: Parent chains in a DFS forest end at a forest root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. Say that $p$ is a recorded parent of $c$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, and call a discovered vertex with no recorded parent a forest root. Then for every vertex $v$ in the discovery order (preorder) there are $k \ge 0$ and vertices…

results.title: The DFS parent relation is acyclic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. Say that $p$ is a recorded parent of $c$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search. Then there are no $k \ge 1$ and vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ with $v_k = v_0$ such that each $v_{i+1}$ is a recorded parent of $v_i$.

results.title: DFS forest roots are scheduled roots
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex. If $v$ is a forest root of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$, then $v$ occurs in $r$.

results.title: Depth-first search of the whole graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph traversal is the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$, taken in the graph's fixed vertex enumeration order.

results.title: Whole-graph DFS discovers every vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the preorder of the whole-graph depth-first search of $G$, that is, the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.

results.title: Whole-graph DFS finishes every vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the postorder of the whole-graph depth-first search of $G$, that is, the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.

results.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph decreasing finish order is the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$, taken in the graph's vertex enumeration order; its vertices are listed from the latest finished to the earliest finished.

results.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order contains every vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the whole-graph decreasing finish order of $G$, that is, the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.

results.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph decreasing finish order of $G$ contains no vertex twice.

results.title: Exact transition count of depth-first search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists $N(v)$, whose entries may repeat, and let $R$ be a list of roots, possibly with repetitions. Run the depth-first search machine from $R$ (each transition drops a pending vertex that is already visited, discovers a new vertex, or finishes a vertex). Let $v_1, \dots, v_k$ be the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$. Then there is a terminal…

results.title: Exact transition count of whole-graph depth-first search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph whose vertices are listed without repetition as $v_1, \dots, v_n$, with ordered adjacency lists $N(v)$ whose entries may repeat. Run the depth-first search machine with roots $v_1, \dots, v_n$ in this order (each transition drops a pending vertex that is already visited, discovers a new vertex, or finishes a vertex). Then there is a terminal machine state, with no work left, whose…

results.title: Indegree within a vertex list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite directed graph $G$, a list $R$ of vertices and a vertex $v$, the indegree of $v$ within $R$ is the number of entries $u$ of $R$, counted with multiplicity, such that $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$.

results.title: Indegree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The indegree of a vertex $v$ in a finite directed graph $G$ is the number of vertices $u$ such that $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$; repeated entries in adjacency lists count once.

results.title: Outcome of Kahn's topological sort
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The result of Kahn's topological sorting algorithm on a graph with vertices of type $\alpha$ is either a success, carrying a list of vertices, or a failure, carrying the list of vertices processed before the queue emptied and the list of vertices that remain.

results.title: Kahn's topological sort
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Run Kahn's algorithm with a first-in first-out queue on a finite directed graph $G$ whose vertices are enumerated as $v_1, \dots, v_n$. Initially every vertex is remaining, the counter of each vertex is its number of in-neighbours, and the queue holds the vertices with no in-neighbours in enumeration order. At each of $n$ steps, if the queue is nonempty, its front vertex $x$ is removed from the queue and from the…

results.title: Directed cycle within a vertex list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of vertices. A list $c = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of vertices is a directed cycle of $G$ in $R$ when $k \ge 1$, the vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$ are pairwise distinct, $G$ has an edge from $c_i$ to $c_{i+1}$ for each $1 \le i < k$ and an edge from $c_k$ to $c_1$, and every $c_i$ lies in $R$.

results.title: Characterization of directed cycles within a vertex list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and let $R$ and $c = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ be lists of vertices. Then $c$ is a directed cycle of $G$ in $R$ if and only if $k \ge 1$, the vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$ are pairwise distinct, $G$ has an edge from $c_i$ to $c_{i+1}$ for every $1 \le i < k$, $G$ has an edge from $c_k$ to $c_1$, and every $c_i$ lies in $R$.

results.title: Acyclic directed graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite directed graph $G$ is acyclic when it has no directed cycle, that is, no nonempty list $[c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of pairwise distinct vertices such that $G$ has an edge from $c_i$ to $c_{i+1}$ for each $1 \le i < k$ and an edge from $c_k$ to $c_1$.

results.title: Acyclicity means having no directed cycle
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A finite directed graph $G$ is acyclic if and only if there is no directed cycle of $G$ in its vertex list, that is, no nonempty list of pairwise distinct vertices in which each vertex has an edge to the next and the last vertex has an edge to the first.

results.title: Topological order
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A list $L$ of vertices of a finite directed graph $G$ is a topological order of $G$ when $L$ has no duplicates, a vertex lies in $L$ exactly when it lies in the vertex enumeration of $G$, and for every edge $u \to v$ of $G$ the first position of $u$ in $L$ is strictly smaller than the first position of $v$ in $L$.

results.title: A successful topological sort has no repeated vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then $L$ has no duplicates.

results.title: A successful topological sort lists every vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then a vertex lies in $L$ if and only if it lies in the vertex enumeration of $G$.

results.title: A successful topological sort points every edge forward
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then for every edge $u \to v$ of $G$ the first position of $u$ in $L$ is strictly smaller than the first position of $v$ in $L$.

results.title: A successful topological sort is a topological order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then $L$ is a topological order of $G$.

results.title: A failed Kahn run splits the vertices into processed and unprocessed ones
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph. If deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails after processing the vertex list $P$ and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then $R$ is nonempty, neither $P$ nor $R$ has repeated entries, a vertex lies in the vertex list of $G$ if and only if it lies in $P$ or in $R$, and no vertex lies in both $P$ and $R$.

results.title: Unprocessed vertices of a failed Kahn run have positive indegree among the unprocessed
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph. If deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails after processing the vertex list $P$ and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then for every vertex $v$ in $R$ the indegree of $v$ within $R$, the number of entries $u$ of $R$ such that $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$, is positive.

results.title: A failed Kahn run leaves a directed cycle
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph. If deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails after processing the vertex list $P$ and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then $G$ has a directed cycle in $R$: a nonempty list of pairwise distinct vertices of $R$ in which each vertex has an edge to the next and the last vertex has an edge to the first.

results.title: Success of Kahn's algorithm implies acyclicity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success, then $G$ is acyclic.

results.title: Kahn's algorithm succeeds on acyclic graphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a finite directed graph $G$, given by a vertex enumeration and adjacency lists, is acyclic, then deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ returns success with some vertex order.

results.title: Kahn's algorithm succeeds exactly on acyclic graphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$, Kahn's topological sort on $G$ returns a success if and only if $G$ is acyclic.
